item.title: mfa — enough factors, and which ones
item.description:
Did enough factors answer, of enough kinds — and which ones? Nothing here reaches a device, and there is no cryptography: a Factor is anything that can be asked is this person here, now?, and this package decides what the answers add up to.

go get github.com/go-authn/mfa@v0.5.0

It imports nothing outside the standard library.

Two of the same thing is one factor

A passphrase and a recovery code are both things the person knows: whoever learned one has usually learned the other from the same place. So a factor says what it proves — Knowledge, Possession or Inherence — and the policy that means what two-factor is normally taken to mean isPolicy{Count: 2, DistinctKinds: true}. Policy{Count: 2} alone is also offered, for a caller who wants two keys of the same kind on purpose; it is a different request and is spelled differently.

A factor whose Kind() is Unknown counts towards the number satisfied, never towards the kinds: it cannot be shown to differ from anything.

Example 

package main

import (
 "context"
 "errors"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/mfa"
)

// factor is the smallest mfa.Factor: a name, a kind, and an answer.
type factor struct {
 name string
 kind mfa.Kind
 err error
}

func (f factor) Name() string { return f.name }
func (f factor) Kind() mfa.Kind { return f.kind }
func (f factor) Verify(context.Context) error { return f.err }

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()
 twoFactor := mfa.Policy{Count: 2, DistinctKinds: true}

 // Two things the person knows are one kind of proof.
 _, err := mfa.Verify(ctx, twoFactor,
 factor{"your passphrase", mfa.Knowledge, nil},
 factor{"a recovery code", mfa.Knowledge, nil},
 )
 fmt.Println(err)

 // A key that is not plugged in has not refused anybody.
 r, err := mfa.Verify(ctx, twoFactor,
 factor{"your passphrase", mfa.Knowledge, nil},
 factor{"your security key", mfa.Possession, mfa.Unavailable(errors.New("no key attached"))},
 )
 fmt.Println(err)
 fmt.Println(r.Answers[1].Unavailable())

 // The zero Policy is refused, not guessed at.
 _, err = mfa.Verify(ctx, mfa.Policy{}, factor{"your passphrase", mfa.Knowledge, nil})
 fmt.Println(err)
}
mfa: 2 factor(s) answered but only 1 kind(s) among them (knowledge); two of the same kind are not two factors
mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your security key (possession): not available
true
mfa: a policy that requires 0 factors accepts anyone

The real factors live elsewhere: totp for a code from a phone, keyfactor for a security key.

What it refuses, and why

Verify refuses before it asks anybody:

why
a Policy whose Count is below one a policy that requires 0 factors accepts anyone. There is no default policy: how much proof is enough belongs to whoever protects the thing
fewer factors offered than Count the policy cannot be met, whatever they answer
a factor whose Kind() is outside the enumeration counted as a distinct kind, Kind(42) beside a passphrase would pass as two-factor
the same factor twice before v0.3.0, one passphrase passed twice satisfied Count: 2, and before v0.4.0 so did any factor holding a function. “The same” is the same type holding the same values, functions included: a function is the same function when it runs the same code

And it keeps three things apart while it asks:

  • Could not be asked is not a refusal. A factor that returnsErrUnavailable — wrapped by mfa.Unavailable(err), which keeps the reason — is reported as such (Answer.Unavailable()), and never ends an attempt even with StopOnFirstFailure.
  • Every factor is asked by default, so a person can be told your key answered, your fingerprint did not in one attempt. StopOnFirstFailure is there when stopping early is wanted.
  • A factor not reached has no entry in Result.Answers: reporting it as failed would send somebody after nothing.

The Result is returned whether or not the policy was met, with the error naming what was missing in words a person can act on.

What it is checked against

No external judge: the module holds no protocol to disagree with. Its CI requires 100% statement coverage on Linux, macOS and Windows, runs the race detector, and runs the tests on amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x,386 and arm.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/mfa@v0.5.0

item.title: totp — a code, once, and not a million guesses
item.description:
Is this six-digit code right — and has it been used before? Time-based one-time passwords (RFC 6238); a Verifier that remembers what a server has to, the codes already used and the wrong ones; and a factor that anmfa policy can ask for.

go get github.com/go-authn/totp@v0.4.2

Its one dependency is go-authn/mfa.

The defaults are what every phone assumes: six digits, every 30 seconds,HMAC-SHA1, one step of tolerance either side. Options changes Digits,Period, Algorithm (SHA1, SHA256, SHA512) and Window.

Example 

package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/totp"
)

func main() {
 secret, err := totp.ParseSecret("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP")
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 now := time.Date(2026, 10, 10, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
 o := totp.Options{Now: func() time.Time { return now }}

 code, _ := totp.At(secret, now, o) // what the phone shows
 fmt.Println(code)

 v := &totp.Verifier{Options: o}
 fmt.Println(v.Verify("dora", secret, []byte(code))) // accepted
 fmt.Println(v.Verify("dora", secret, []byte(code))) // the same code again
 fmt.Println(v.Verify("Dora", secret, []byte(code))) // another spelling, same secret

 // A secret shorter than 128 bits makes no code.
 short, _ := totp.ParseSecret("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP")
 _, err = totp.At(short, now, o)
 fmt.Println(err)
}
395621
<nil>
totp: that code has already been used
totp: that code has already been used
totp: a secret of 80 bits; RFC 4226 requires at least 128

In a policy, the code becomes a factor of kind Possession, next to whatever checks the password:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/mfa"
 "github.com/go-authn/totp"
)

// knows stands in for whatever checks the password.
type knows struct{}

func (knows) Name() string { return "your password" }
func (knows) Kind() mfa.Kind { return mfa.Knowledge }
func (knows) Verify(context.Context) error { return nil }

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()
 secret, _ := totp.ParseSecret("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP")
 verifier := &totp.Verifier{} // one per server, kept: it remembers used codes
 code := []byte("123456") // what the person typed

 _, err := mfa.Verify(ctx, mfa.Policy{Count: 2, DistinctKinds: true},
 knows{},
 totp.Factor("dora", secret, code, verifier),
 )
 fmt.Println(err)
}
mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code is not right

A code read aloud over the telephone is possession no longer; the classification is what DistinctKinds relies on.

What it refuses, and why

A code already accepted. RFC 6238 §5.2: the verifier MUST NOT accept a second attempt of an OTP that already succeeded. The stateless totp.Verify cannot — it holds nothing between calls — so a server uses a *Verifier, which refuses with ErrUsed every step up to and including the last one it accepted: a code from thirty seconds ago is still inside the default window.

A Factor without a Verifier. totp.Factor with a nil *Verifier refuses every code, saying a Verifier is missing. It is not reported as unavailable, so a policy cannot pass on the other factors and hide the mistake.

Guessing, per secret. A Verifier counts wrong codes per credential —the secret, held only as its SHA-256 — not per name, because the name is whatever string the caller passes, and before v0.3.0 dora, Dora and DORA were three counters for one secret.

field default
Throttle DefaultThrottle = 5 wrong codes in a row before ErrThrottled; the code sent meanwhile is not looked at, so not even the right one passes
Pause DefaultPause = 15 minutes how long that lasts
Lockout DefaultLockout = 100 wrong codes in a row, however spread out, before ErrLockedOut, which only Forget lifts (NIST SP 800-63B §5.2.2)

Only a wrong code counts; a replay, a code of the wrong length or a refused parameter does not bring a pause nearer. The whole check is made under one lock, so guesses sent at the same moment are counted one by one.ErrLockedOut wraps ErrThrottled, so errors.Is(err, totp.ErrThrottled) is true for both refusals, and errors.Is(err, totp.ErrLockedOut) only for the lockout.

Parameters that cannot be right:

  • a secret under 128 bits (MinSecret = 16 bytes, RFC 4226 R6), inGenerate, At, Verify and Verifier.Verify. ParseSecret still reads one: it is a parser;
  • a period that is not a whole number of seconds, or under one second;
  • fewer than 6 or more than 10 digits (RFC 4226 §5.3);
  • a window wider than MaxWindow = 10 steps either side. 0 means the default of one step; NoWindow accepts only the current step.

Every step in the window is tried without stopping early, and the comparison is constant-time. ErrWrongCode is the same error for “wrong” and “too old”.

The secret is the credential

Whoever holds it produces every future code. No error message here quotes a code or a secret, and URI — the otpauth:// string an authenticator reads from a QR code — carries the secret by construction: it is for the person enrolling, and nobody else.

The Verifier’s memory is this process’s. Two servers behind a load balancer each refuse their own replays and count their own guesses; a deployment that needs one answer puts a shared store behind the same interface.

What it is checked against

  • pyotp, a Python implementation: 200 random cases across secret lengths from 16 bytes, 6 to 10 digits, four periods and all three algorithms(differential_test.go). The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install it, and there TOTP_REQUIRE_JUDGE turns a missing pyotp into a failure rather than a skip.
  • RFC 6238 Appendix B, all six times and all three algorithms, andRFC 4226 Appendix D, counters 0 to 9.
  • Every digit count over 1000 steps per algorithm, against RFC 4226 §5.3 recomputed in arbitrary precision.

The coverage lane fails below 95% (its stated standard is 100%), and the tests run on eight architectures.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/totp@v0.4.2

item.title: fido — speaking to a security key
item.description:
How is a security key spoken to? The FIDO client-to-authenticator protocol— the CTAPHID framing, the channel handshake, and the CTAP2 commands that register a credential, ask for a signature and exchange a PIN for a token — in pure Go, on any operating system.

go get github.com/go-authn/fido@v0.6.2

Nothing here is platform-specific. A Transport moves 64-byte reports to and from one authenticator and says what the device is called; where those reports come from — IOKit on macOS, hidraw on Linux, WebHID in a browser — is somebody else’s package. Everything above it is here:
Open(ctx, t) the INIT handshake on the broadcast channel; returns a *Key with its own channel. The Key owns t: Close closes it, and so does a failed Open
Key.Ping, Key.Wink a round trip, and a blink — the cheapest way to ask which of these keys is this one?
Key.GetInfo versions, extensions, AAGUID, options, PIN protocols
Key.MakeCredential, Key.GetAssertion register, and sign; ParseAuthData reads the authenticator data, and AuthData.PublicKey turns a P-256 COSE key into an *ecdsa.PublicKey
Key.PINRetries, Key.KeyAgreement, Key.PINToken authenticatorClientPIN, both PIN/UV auth protocols
Split, NewReassembler, ParseInit, Key.CBOR the framing, exported for whoever drives a key some other way

AuthData.PublicKey is a conversion, not a verification: which algorithms count and what to do with a sign counter that went backwards belongs to the caller. keyfactor is one such caller.

Example

The framing alone, with no key: a message cut into reports, and put back together.

package main

import (
 "bytes"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/fido"
)

func main() {
 // A 200-byte ping, cut into the 64-byte reports a key reads...
 payload := bytes.Repeat([]byte{0xA5}, 200)
 reports, err := fido.Split(0x01020304, fido.CmdPing, payload)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 fmt.Println(len(reports), "reports of", len(reports[0]), "bytes")

 // ...and put back together, as a reply would be.
 r := fido.NewReassembler(0x01020304)
 for _, rep := range reports {
 msg, done, err := r.Feed(rep)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 if done {
 fmt.Println(bytes.Equal(msg.Data, payload), msg.Cmd == fido.CmdPing)
 }
 }

 // A report for another channel is an error, not something to drop.
 other, _ := fido.Split(0x0A0B0C0D, fido.CmdPing, []byte("hi"))
 _, _, err = fido.NewReassembler(0x01020304).Feed(other[0])
 fmt.Println(err)

 // The framing's real limit, not the length field's.
 fmt.Println(fido.MaxMessage)
}
4 reports of 64 bytes
true true
fido: the report belongs to another channel
7609

With a key, fido.Open(ctx, transport) does the handshake and the *Key it returns carries every later command.

What it refuses, and why

A key is not trusted to answer what it was asked. A reply that carries a different command from the one sent is refused (CTAP 2.1 §11.2.9 gives each response its own command, and libfido2 checks it too). An INIT reply whose nonce is not the one sent is refused: it is another program’s handshake on the same key. A PIN token that is not its protocol’s length — 16 or 32 bytes under protocol one, exactly 32 under protocol two — is refused.

A keepalive is not an answer. A key waiting for a finger sendsCTAPHID_KEEPALIVE about every hundred milliseconds; it is skipped, and the only bound on how long a touch may take is the context.

A message longer than the framing can carry. Two length bytes would allow 65535, but 57 bytes in the initialisation packet plus 128 continuations of 59 is 7609 (MaxMessage); past that a sequence number would reach 0x80 and a key would read it as a new message. Split returns ErrTooLong.

Reports that do not add up: one for another channel (ErrWrongChannel —two programs on one key), continuations out of order (ErrOutOfOrder), a report shorter than a packet (ErrShortPacket), an INIT reply shorter than its 17 bytes (ErrTruncated).

A command the key did not say it supports. Wink is not sent to a key without CapWink, nor GetInfo to one without CapCBOR: the key would answerCTAPHID_ERROR, and the caller would have to tell that refusal from a fault.

An empty PIN, and anything but P-256 in AuthData.PublicKey — refused by name rather than half-decoded.

A wrong PIN costs a retry

CTAP gives an authenticator a counter of PIN retries, eight at most, and each wrong PIN spends one. Three wrong PINs in a row block the PIN until the key is unplugged and plugged back in. A counter that reaches zero blocks it for good:only a reset lifts that, and a reset erases every credential on the key. AskKey.PINRetries before prompting anybody: it says how many retries are left,and whether the key is waiting to be unplugged.

When a key refuses a PIN, the error says which of the two it is.CTAP2_ERR_PIN_AUTH_BLOCKED (0x34), which unplugging lifts, readstoo many wrong PINs in a row; unplug the key and plug it in again (0x34);CTAP2_ERR_PIN_BLOCKED (0x32), which only a reset lifts, readsthe PIN is blocked: no tries are left, and only a reset, which erases the credentials, unblocks it (0x32).Before v0.6.2 the two sentences were swapped: a key that only had to be unplugged was called locked, and somebody told that might reset it and lose every credential on it.

What it is checked against

The CI has no security key, so the tests use a fake transport that reassembles what it is sent — a key that refuses, stalls, keeps saying it is busy, or shares its channel with another program — with coverage held at 100%. Two fixtures come from outside this code:

  • testdata/yubikey-fido-5.7.4-getinfo.hex, the GetInfo reply captured from a YubiKey FIDO 5.7.4, decoded by ctap2_test.go;
  • testdata/webauthn-reference-authdata.b64, a sample from the tests ofgo-webauthn/webauthn, which checks the authenticator-data parser andAuthData.PublicKey.

The status-code table follows libfido2’s err.h. The module’s README records a registration and an assertion run against a real YubiKey, with the signature verified against the public key it handed out; that run is not part of CI.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/fido@v0.6.2

item.title: keyfactor — the registered key, touched
item.description:
Did the key that was registered answer, and did a person touch it? keyfactor is the one piece between fido,which speaks CTAP and knows about no policy, andmfa, which decides how much proof is enough and knows about no device. Neither imports the other; this imports both.

go get github.com/go-authn/keyfactor@v0.4.2

At v0.4.2 its go.mod requires at least go-authn/fido v0.6.2 andgo-authn/mfa v0.5.0, the versions these pages describe.

The platform supplies an Opener — how a key is found on this system — and keeps only that. Everything else is the same wherever CTAP is: the assertion,the checks, the refusal to spend somebody’s last PIN attempt.

Example 

package main

import (
 "context"
 "crypto/ecdsa"
 "errors"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/fido"
 "github.com/go-authn/keyfactor"
 "github.com/go-authn/mfa"
)

func main() {
 // The platform supplies the Opener: how a key is found on this system.
 // This one finds nothing, and says so the way a policy understands.
 open := func(context.Context) (fido.Transport, error) {
 return nil, keyfactor.Unavailable(errors.New("no security key is plugged in"))
 }

 // From the registration: the credential ID and its public key, which
 // fido.AuthData.PublicKey returns from the attestation.
 var pub *ecdsa.PublicKey // nil here, to show the refusal

 f := keyfactor.New(open, keyfactor.Options{
 RPID: "example.test",
 CredentialID: []byte{0x01, 0x02},
 PublicKey: pub,
 })
 fmt.Println(f.Name(), f.Kind())

 _, err := mfa.Verify(context.Background(), mfa.Policy{Count: 1}, f)
 fmt.Println(err)
}
your security key possession
mfa: 1 factor(s) needed, 0 answered: your security key (possession): keyfactor: no public key for the credential; without one any device that answers would pass, so pass the one from the registration

The refusal comes before the Opener is called. With the registration’s public key, the same factor opens the key, asks it for an assertion over a fresh random challenge, and checks the answer.

What it refuses, and why

A device answering is not the key answering. A programmable USB board speaks CTAP as well as a security key does, so the answer is checked against the registration:

refused message
before anything is opened: no Opener, no RPID, no PublicKey, or a key not on P-256 keyfactor: no opener; …, … needs a relying party id …, … no public key for the credential; …, … is not on P-256 …
a relying-party hash that is not SHA-256 of RPID … answered for another relying party
a credential other than CredentialID, when the device names one … answered with a credential other than the one asked for
a signature over the authenticator data and the challenge that PublicKey did not make … answered with a signature the credential's key did not make
no UP flag … answered without anyone touching it
no UV flag when a PIN was given … was asked to establish who holds it and did not

The last PIN attempt is not spent on a guess. PINRetries is asked first;a key that will take no more PINs until it is unplugged is refused, and so is one with one attempt or fewer left. Under CTAP, three wrong PINs in a row block a key’s PIN until it is unplugged, and a retry counter that reaches zero blocks it for good: only a reset lifts that, erasing every credential on it.

When the key itself refuses a PIN, the error is fido’s, and from fido v0.6.2 it names the right one of the two:too many wrong PINs in a row; unplug the key and plug it in again (0x34) when unplugging lifts the block, andthe PIN is blocked: no tries are left, and only a reset, which erases the credentials, unblocks it (0x32) when only a reset does. Before fido v0.6.2 the two sentences were swapped.

A PIN is not a second factor. The kind stays mfa.Possession: a PIN entered into the key protects the key, and identifies nobody to this machine.

An empty port is not a refusal. An Opener that finds nothing wraps its error with keyfactor.Unavailable, which marks it mfa.ErrUnavailable, and a policy counts could not be asked apart from said no.

What it cannot protect: the PIN’s hash reaches whatever device answers

CTAP has the platform hand the key LEFT(SHA-256(PIN), 16), encrypted under a secret agreed with the device itself, before anything is signed. A forged device is refused as a factor, but it has received that hash, and a short PIN falls to an offline search. That is the protocol. Use a long PIN, and do not type one into a key whose provenance is unknown.

What it is checked against

The tests fake the authenticator, not the transport, built from go-authn/fido’s own exported framing: a CTAPHID handshake, a CTAP2 assertion,and a ClientPIN exchange. The PIN half plays the authenticator’s side of protocol two independently — its own ECDH, HKDF and AES-CBC, written from the specification (fakepin_test.go) — so a derivation that differed by a byte would fail the exchange. forged_test.go is the device that holds no credential. Coverage is held at 100%, and the tests run on eight architectures.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/keyfactor@v0.4.2
